text: Distinguish a layer-4 load balancer from a layer-7 one: what each can see about a request, and one routing decision only the layer-7 one can make. Then explain what a health check has to verify for the load balancer to be useful during a partial failure.

expected_concepts.hint: L4 sees addresses and ports; L7 terminates the connection and sees the request
path, host or header based routing needs L7
the check must exercise the dependencies the request path actually uses
a process can accept connections while being unable to serve them

common_misconceptions: believes a TCP connect check is sufficient evidence that an instance is healthy
assumes layer-7 routing is always preferable, ignoring its per-request cost
reference_answer: A layer-4 balancer works at the transport layer: it sees IP addresses, ports and connection state, and forwards packets or connections without interpreting their contents. It is fast, protocol-agnostic and cheap, and it can do little more than spread connections. A layer-7 balancer terminates the connection and parses the application protocol, so it sees the path, method, headers, cookies and body size. That lets it do things L4 cannot: route /api to one pool and /static to another, split traffic by header for a canary release, retry an idempotent request on another instance, or terminate TLS and enforce per-route rate limits. The cost is CPU per request and a component that understands your protocol. On health checks, the point is that a TCP connect only proves a process is listening. An instance whose database pool is exhausted, whose disk is full, or whose dependency is down will happily accept connections and fail every request - and the balancer will keep sending it traffic. A useful check is an HTTP endpoint that exercises the real dependencies, with a timeout, checked frequently enough to remove a bad instance in seconds. The counterweight is that a check which is too strict makes a shared dependency's blip remove the entire fleet at once, so a readiness check that fails on a dependency and a liveness check that only reflects the process itself should be kept separate.

text: Sticky sessions pin a user to one backend instance for the duration of their session. Explain the problem they solve, three things they make worse - for deployments, for scaling and during a failure - and the design change that removes the need for them.

expected_concepts.hint: routing a user back to the instance holding their in-process state
move session state to a shared store or a signed token and affinity becomes unnecessary
replacing an instance destroys the sessions it held
losing one instance logs out exactly the users pinned to it

common_misconceptions: treats sticky sessions as a load-balancing optimisation rather than a workaround for state
assumes affinity distributes load evenly regardless of how long sessions last
reference_answer: Sticky sessions exist because the instance is holding state the next request needs - a session object, an in-process cache, an open upload or a WebSocket. If that state lives only in one process, any other instance would fail the request, so the balancer must send the user back to the same one. What it costs: deployments become destructive, since replacing an instance discards the sessions on it, so a rolling deploy logs users out or forces long connection-draining windows. Scaling stops working properly, because a new instance only receives new sessions and existing long-lived ones stay where they are, so load skews and adding capacity does not relieve the hot instance. Failure becomes user-visible in a targeted way: losing one instance does not degrade everyone slightly, it breaks completely for the fraction of users pinned to it. Affinity also defeats even distribution generally, since sessions differ in weight and duration. The fix is to make the service stateless: put session data in a shared store such as Redis or the database, or in a signed token the client carries, so any instance can serve any request. Then the balancer is free to route anywhere, deploys and autoscaling become routine, and losing an instance costs one retry. Where affinity is genuinely unavoidable - a live WebSocket, or a local cache whose hit rate is worth real money - it should be a deliberate, documented exception with a plan for what happens when the instance dies.
follow_up_seeds: What are the tradeoffs between a shared session store and a signed token?

text: A team wants to run their API on ten instances behind a load balancer instead of one. List the kinds of state that currently live inside the process and would break under that change, and say where each kind should move to instead.

expected_concepts.hint: any request must be servable by any instance
sessions and uploaded files move to a shared store or object storage
ten local caches invalidate independently and disagree
an in-process scheduler now runs ten times; needs a lock or a real queue

common_misconceptions: considers only session state and forgets timers, local files and in-memory counters
assumes a local cache is harmless because it is only an optimisation
reference_answer: The rule is that any instance must be able to serve any request, so anything held in one process is a problem. Sessions: move to Redis or the database, or replace with a signed token the client carries. Uploaded files and generated artefacts written to local disk: move to object storage, since a later request may land elsewhere and a container filesystem does not survive a restart anyway. In-memory caches: each instance will now hold its own copy and invalidate independently, so users see different data depending on where they land; move to a shared cache, or keep the local cache deliberately with a short TTL and accept a bounded inconsistency. In-process counters, rate limiters and de-duplication sets: these silently become ten separate counters, so a 100-per-minute limit becomes 1000; move the counter to a shared store. Scheduled jobs and background timers: an in-process cron now fires ten times, sending duplicate emails; move to a job queue with a single consumer group, or guard with a distributed lock or leader election. WebSocket and SSE connections: these terminate on one instance, so broadcasting requires a pub/sub layer between instances. Finally, anything the process assumed was serialised by being single-threaded on one machine now needs real concurrency control in the database. A practical way to find all of it is to run two instances locally and route round-robin between them; every one of these bugs shows up immediately.
follow_up_seeds: Which of these would you fix first, and why that one?

text: Compare scaling a service vertically with scaling it horizontally. Give one workload where vertical scaling is genuinely the better engineering decision, and name the limit that eventually forces a horizontal approach.

expected_concepts.hint: a bigger machine versus more machines
the largest available instance, and a superlinear price curve before it
distribution buys capacity by adding coordination, partial failure and consistency questions
one machine is one point of failure, however large it is

common_misconceptions: treats horizontal scaling as strictly superior in all situations
ignores that a vertical resize usually requires a restart
reference_answer: Vertical scaling means giving the same instance more CPU, memory or faster storage. It is simple - no code changes, no coordination, and the program keeps its single-process assumptions - and it is often the cheapest fix for a real problem in engineer-hours. Horizontal scaling means running more instances behind a balancer, which is what gives near-unbounded capacity and, importantly, redundancy. Vertical is genuinely better for a stateful single-writer system: a primary relational database is the standard example, because sharding it introduces cross-shard joins, distributed transactions and a rebalancing problem, whereas doubling its memory so the working set fits in cache may buy a year of headroom for a day of work. The same argument applies to a workload that is hard to parallelise, such as a single large in-memory computation. The limits that force horizontal are: the largest instance available is a hard ceiling; price rises superlinearly well before that ceiling; resizing usually needs a restart, so scaling itself causes downtime; and one machine is one failure domain, so no amount of vertical scaling gives availability. That last point is the important one - horizontal scaling is often adopted for redundancy rather than for throughput, and a system that must survive the loss of a machine has to be horizontal regardless of its load. In practice the sequence is to scale up first, and out when capacity, cost or availability demands it.
follow_up_seeds: What would make you scale out before you had to?

text: A multi-tenant application shards its main table by tenant_id. Explain why this key usually works well, describe the failure mode when one tenant is a hundred times larger than every other, and outline what re-sharding would involve while the service stays online.

expected_concepts.hint: the key should match the query boundary so most queries hit one shard
a skewed key makes one shard the bottleneck while others idle
dual write, backfill, verify, cut over reads, then stop the old writes
limits how much data moves when the shard count changes

common_misconceptions: assumes a hash of the key removes skew, when the skew is in the data volume per key
treats re-sharding as a maintenance window rather than a migration process
reference_answer: tenant_id works well because it matches the natural query boundary: almost every query in a multi-tenant application is scoped to one tenant, so it can be routed to a single shard and answered there without any cross-shard join or distributed transaction. It also gives clean isolation and simple per-tenant backup, export and deletion. The failure mode is skew. Shards are balanced by key count, not by data or traffic, so a tenant a hundred times larger puts a hundred times the load on one shard: it hits capacity while the others idle, adding shards does not help because that one tenant cannot be split, and hashing the key does not help either, since the imbalance is inside a single key. Mitigations are to give the largest tenants dedicated shards, to sub-shard a large tenant by a secondary key such as user or time, and to track per-shard size and traffic so the skew is seen before it is an incident. Re-sharding online is a migration, not a switch: stand up the new topology; dual-write to old and new so no writes are lost; backfill historical data in batches; verify by comparing both copies, ideally with a shadow-read comparison in production; move reads over gradually, per tenant or by percentage, with a fast way back; and only when reads have been stable stop writing to the old shard and drop it. Consistent hashing or a lookup table mapping tenant to shard makes this far cheaper than modulo-based placement, where changing the shard count moves nearly every row - and an explicit lookup table has the advantage of allowing a single tenant to be moved on its own.

text: Compare a fixed-window rate limiter with a token bucket for an API allowing 100 requests per minute: describe the burst behaviour each permits, including the boundary problem the fixed window has. Then explain what changes when the limit must be enforced across ten API servers.

expected_concepts.hint: tokens refill at a steady rate; bucket depth is the permitted burst
a counter reset on a clock boundary; cheap but coarse
the fixed window allows 200 requests across a boundary in two seconds
per-instance counters multiply the limit; shared state costs a round trip

common_misconceptions: believes a fixed window enforces an even rate rather than a per-window total
implements per-instance limits and expects the global limit to hold
reference_answer: A fixed window keeps a counter per key that resets on a clock boundary: increment, reject above 100, reset at the top of the minute. It is trivial to implement and cheap to store, but it only bounds the total per window, not the rate. The boundary problem follows directly: a client can send 100 requests at 11:59:59 and 100 more at 12:00:00, so 200 requests arrive in two seconds while every window is technically within limit. A token bucket instead refills tokens at 100 per minute up to a maximum depth, and each request spends one. Because the refill is continuous, the sustained rate is enforced smoothly and the burst is bounded explicitly by the bucket depth, which is a parameter you choose rather than an accident of clock alignment. Sliding window log and sliding window counter sit in between: more accurate than fixed, cheaper than a log. Across ten servers, the state is the whole problem. Ten independent local counters mean each allows 100, so the real limit is 1000 - the most common production mistake here. The correct approach is to hold the counter in a shared store, updated atomically: an INCR with an expiry, or a token bucket implemented as a small Lua script in Redis so the read-modify-write cannot interleave. That adds a network round trip to every request and makes the store a dependency of the request path, so decide what happens when it is unreachable - fail open, which risks overload, or fail closed, which turns a cache outage into an API outage. Where the round trip is too expensive, give each instance a local allowance of the global budget and reconcile periodically, accepting approximate enforcement.
follow_up_seeds: Should the limiter fail open or fail closed when Redis is unreachable?

text: Explain why a public API needs rate limiting even when raw capacity is not a concern. Then say what a well-behaved API should return to a client that has exceeded its limit, including the header that tells the client when to try again.

expected_concepts.hint: fairness between clients, abuse and cost control, not only capacity
429 Too Many Requests, distinct from 503, and not a client bug
Retry-After tells the client when the limit resets
limit headers let a well-written client self-throttle instead of retrying blindly

common_misconceptions: returns 403 or 500 for a rate-limited request
assumes rate limiting is purely a capacity control
reference_answer: Capacity is only one reason. Rate limiting provides fairness, so one client's runaway loop does not starve everyone else; it bounds cost, which matters when a request triggers metered work such as an LLM call or an email; it is a control against abuse, credential stuffing and scraping; and it protects downstream dependencies that are smaller than you are, since your API's capacity is not the binding constraint if a third-party service behind it is. It also protects clients from themselves, by turning an accidental infinite loop into a visible error rather than a large bill. The correct response is 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header giving either a delay in seconds or an HTTP date. 429 is specifically 'you are being throttled, this will succeed later' - distinct from 403, which says the request is not permitted at all, and from 503, which says the server is unhealthy. Alongside it, return the limit state on every response, not just on rejections: RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset let a well-written client pace itself rather than discovering the limit by hitting it. The body should name which limit was hit and its scope, since an API usually has several. Finally, document the limits, and make sure the 429 path is cheap - if rejecting costs as much as serving, the limiter does not protect anything.
follow_up_seeds: Should an authenticated and an anonymous client share the same limit?

text: A read-heavy service caches rows from its database. Compare three invalidation strategies - a short TTL, write-through, and explicit invalidation on write - in terms of staleness window, cost on the write path, and what happens the day a new write path forgets to invalidate.

expected_concepts.hint: TTL, write-through and explicit deletion have different failure modes
how long a reader may see an old value, and whether it is bounded
the write updates cache and store together, adding coupling and a failure mode
explicit invalidation requires every writer, present and future, to remember

common_misconceptions: believes explicit invalidation is strictly better because it is the most immediate
treats a TTL as a correctness mechanism rather than a bound on staleness
reference_answer: A short TTL is the most robust because it needs no cooperation from the write path: any writer, including a manual SQL update or a batch job, is automatically correct within the TTL. Staleness is bounded but never zero, and the TTL is a direct dial between freshness and load - halving it roughly doubles the miss rate. Write-through updates the cache and the database on the same write path, so reads after a write are fresh, at the cost of write latency, and it introduces a partial failure to think about: if the database write succeeds and the cache write does not, the cache is wrong until something else corrects it, which is why write-through is usually paired with a TTL as a backstop. Explicit invalidation - delete the key on write, let the next read repopulate - gives the smallest staleness window and the lowest steady-state write cost, and has the worst failure mode: it is coupled to every write path that will ever exist. A new endpoint, a background job, an admin script or another service writing the same table will silently leave stale data forever, and the bug appears long after the change that caused it, on the one key nobody is looking at. In practice the right answer is usually a combination: invalidate explicitly for immediacy, and keep a TTL so that a missed invalidation is self-healing rather than permanent. Note also that delete-on-write is safer than update-on-write, because two concurrent writers deleting a key cannot leave the wrong value behind, whereas two writers updating it can interleave.
follow_up_seeds: How would you detect that a cache entry has gone stale in production?

text: A cache is given a fixed memory budget smaller than the dataset it fronts. Explain what an eviction policy decides, contrast LRU with LFU including a workload where each is the wrong choice, and say what a steadily falling hit rate tells you about the working set.

expected_concepts.hint: which entry to discard when the budget is full, as a guess at future access
recency versus frequency, and the workloads that defeat each
the set of data actually being accessed in a window; the cache is useful when it fits
a falling hit rate means the working set has outgrown the budget or the pattern changed

common_misconceptions: believes a larger cache always improves the hit rate proportionally
assumes LRU is universally correct because it is the common default
reference_answer: An eviction policy answers one question: when the budget is full and a new entry arrives, which existing entry is least likely to be needed soon? Every policy is a heuristic for predicting future access from past access. LRU discards the least-recently-used entry, assuming recency predicts reuse. It adapts quickly when the popular set changes, and it is defeated by a large sequential scan - a batch job reading every row once evicts the entire hot set with data that will never be read again, a phenomenon called cache pollution. LFU discards the least-frequently-used entry, which resists that scan because one-off items never accumulate a count. Its weakness is the mirror image: an item that was popular last week keeps a high count and squats in the cache long after interest has moved on, and a genuinely new item struggles to accumulate enough hits to survive. Hence the practical compromises - LFU with decay, segmented LRU, or adaptive policies such as ARC - and hence scan-resistant admission policies that refuse to insert an item until it has been seen more than once. A steadily falling hit rate usually means the working set has outgrown the budget, so entries are being evicted before they are reused; it can also mean the access pattern has flattened, with requests spread over more distinct keys. Distinguish them by looking at distinct-key counts and the reuse distance, because the remedies differ: the first is fixed by more memory or a smaller cached representation, the second by caching at a different layer, since more memory will not help a workload with no reuse.
follow_up_seeds: How would you stop a nightly batch job from evicting the hot set?

text: A popular cache entry with a 60-second TTL expires at peak traffic, and the database immediately receives thousands of identical queries. Name this failure, explain why it is a property of the expiry design rather than of the traffic level, and describe two mitigations and what each one costs.

expected_concepts.hint: expiry synchronises every reader into a simultaneous miss on the same key
concurrent misses each independently do the expensive recomputation
one request recomputes under a lock; the others wait for or reuse its result
refresh slightly early with a random chance, so misses do not align

common_misconceptions: proposes a longer TTL, which reduces the frequency of the stampede but not its size
believes adding database capacity is a fix rather than a way to survive it
reference_answer: This is a cache stampede, sometimes called dog-piling, and the concurrent recomputation is a thundering herd. It is caused by the expiry design because a TTL makes the entry vanish at one instant for every reader simultaneously; from that instant until the first recomputation completes, every arriving request misses, and each one independently starts the same expensive query. The severity is set by arrival rate multiplied by recomputation time, so a slower query makes it dramatically worse, and a longer TTL makes it rarer but no smaller. It is worst precisely for the hottest keys, which is why it tends to arrive as an outage rather than as degradation. Mitigation one, request coalescing: the first miss takes a lock on the key and recomputes while the others either wait for its result or briefly serve the stale value. This collapses N recomputations into one; the costs are a lock to manage, a decision about what waiters do if the recomputation is slow or fails, and the risk that the lock itself becomes a bottleneck. Mitigation two, probabilistic early expiry: as an entry approaches its TTL, each reader has a small and increasing chance of refreshing it early, so refreshes are spread across time and one unlucky reader pays while everyone else gets a hit. It needs no coordination, and it costs some redundant refreshes and slightly more complex read logic. Related approaches are serving stale content while refreshing in the background, and adding jitter to TTLs so keys written together do not expire together - which is the same class of bug at the level of the whole cache rather than one key.
follow_up_seeds: What happens under coalescing if the recomputation itself fails?

text: One product contains both an account balance and a 'number of likes' counter. Explain which of these needs strong consistency and which tolerates eventual consistency, what 'eventual' actually promises, and what it would cost to demand strong consistency for both.

expected_concepts.hint: every read sees the latest committed write, at the price of coordination
replicas converge if writes stop; no bound on when unless one is stated
derive the requirement from what a stale read would actually cause
consensus adds latency on every write and reduces availability under partition

common_misconceptions: chooses strong consistency everywhere as the safe default without pricing it
reads 'eventual' as 'a second or two' rather than as an unbounded promise of convergence
reference_answer: The balance needs strong consistency, because the decision made from the read has external consequences that cannot be undone: a stale balance permits an overdraft or a double spend, and reconciling that afterwards is a business problem, not a technical one. The like counter tolerates eventual consistency, because a count that is briefly a few behind causes no incorrect decision and no user notices. Eventual consistency promises only convergence: if writes stop, all replicas will agree eventually. It gives no bound on how long, and no guarantee about what a reader sees in the meantime - a read can go backwards, and two users can see different values at the same moment. In practice systems layer stronger session guarantees on top, such as read-your-writes and monotonic reads, because those are what users actually notice. Demanding strong consistency for both costs latency and availability. Every write must be coordinated - a quorum or a consensus round, so a cross-region write carries at least one round trip and often more - and during a network partition the minority side must refuse writes rather than serve them, so availability falls exactly when you need it. It also concentrates writes, which makes the like counter, the highest-volume and least important write in the product, the thing that limits throughput. The point worth making is that consistency is chosen per operation, not per system: the same product can and should run a consensus-backed store for money and an eventually consistent, conflict-free counter for likes.
follow_up_seeds: Which session guarantees would you add to the like counter, and why?

text: State what the P in the CAP theorem actually refers to, and why saying 'we chose AP' is only meaningful as a statement about behaviour during a network partition. Describe what a CP system and an AP system each do with a write request while the partition is happening.

expected_concepts.hint: given a partition, a system must choose between consistency and availability
P is a fault the network imposes, not a property you select
the choice only binds while partitioned; both are available when the network is healthy
decide in advance whether the minority side refuses writes or accepts and reconciles

common_misconceptions: describes CAP as picking two of three properties as a permanent architecture choice
believes a CP system is unavailable in normal operation
reference_answer: P is partition tolerance: the system continues to operate when the network drops or delays messages between nodes. It is not a design option, because networks partition whether or not you planned for them; any distributed system must tolerate partitions in the sense of not corrupting itself. So the theorem is really a conditional: while a partition is in progress, you cannot have both consistency and availability, and you must choose. That is why 'we chose two of three' is the wrong framing and 'we chose AP' only means something about partition behaviour - when the network is healthy, a well-built system is both consistent and available, and CAP says nothing about it. During a partition, a CP system keeps the invariant and sacrifices availability on at least one side: the minority partition cannot form a quorum, so it rejects or blocks writes, and typically reads too if they must be linearisable. Clients there get errors or timeouts, and no divergent history is created. An AP system accepts writes on both sides, so both remain available and their histories diverge; when the partition heals it must merge them, using last-write-wins, vector clocks, CRDTs or application-level resolution - and last-write-wins silently discards data, which is a decision, not a default. Two things are worth adding. Availability in CAP is the strict formal notion of every non-failing node answering, which is not the same as an SLA. And PACELC is the more useful extension in practice: else, when there is no partition, you still trade latency against consistency on every single request, which is the tradeoff a system actually lives with the rest of the time.

text: Compare single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication. For each, say where a write may be accepted and what happens when two conflicting writes to the same record are accepted, and name a situation in which multi-leader is worth its conflict-resolution cost.

expected_concepts.hint: all writes go to one node, which orders them, so conflicts cannot arise
several nodes accept writes, so concurrent conflicting writes are possible
clients write to several replicas; R + W > N gives overlap
last-write-wins, version vectors, CRDTs, or asking the application

common_misconceptions: believes multi-leader improves write throughput without introducing conflicts
treats last-write-wins as a resolution strategy rather than as data loss
reference_answer: Single-leader: all writes go to one node, which assigns them an order and streams the log to followers that serve reads. Conflicts are impossible by construction, which is why this is the default and why it is what a standard relational setup does. The costs are that the leader is a write bottleneck and a failover point, and that followers lag. Multi-leader: several nodes accept writes and replicate to each other, so two users can update the same record on different leaders concurrently and neither write can be rejected at the time - the conflict is discovered afterwards, on replication. Resolution options are last-write-wins by timestamp, which is simple and silently discards one user's work and depends on clocks you cannot trust; version vectors, which detect the conflict precisely and hand it to someone to resolve; CRDTs, which are designed so that concurrent updates merge deterministically; or explicit application logic. Leaderless: the client writes to several replicas directly and reads from several, with R + W > N ensuring a read set overlaps the last write set; conflicting versions are returned together or reconciled by read repair, so the same resolution question appears at read time. Multi-leader earns its cost when writes must be accepted locally and cannot wait: multi-region deployments where a cross-ocean round trip per write is unacceptable, and offline-capable clients such as a mobile or collaborative editing application, where each device is effectively a leader that syncs later. In both cases the conflict-resolution work is unavoidable because the alternative - refusing the write - is the thing the design exists to prevent.
follow_up_seeds: Why is last-write-wins particularly dangerous across regions?

text: A service stores user profiles, an append-only audit trail, and uploaded profile images. Recommend a storage technology for each, and justify every choice by the access pattern rather than by the shape of the data.

expected_concepts.hint: read/write ratio, query shape, size per item, retention and durability needs
how the data is queried decides the store, not how it looks
large immutable blobs belong in object storage with a URL in the database
immutable, time-ordered, queried by range and retained cheaply

common_misconceptions: stores image bytes in a database column for transactional convenience
chooses a document store for profiles purely because a profile is a nested object
reference_answer: Profiles: a relational table. The access pattern is point lookup by user id, occasional queries by an indexed attribute, and updates that must be consistent with the rest of the account - which wants transactions, constraints and joins to other user data. A document store is defensible if profiles are genuinely schemaless and always fetched whole, but 'it is a nested object' is the wrong reason on its own, and PostgreSQL's JSONB covers that case without giving up the relational parts. Audit trail: append-only, never updated, written far more often than read, read by time range and by subject, and retained for a long time. That points to a table partitioned by time - so old partitions can be dropped or archived instantly - or to a purpose-built log or time-series store if the volume justifies one. The key properties are cheap sequential appends, range scans, and inexpensive retention, plus the integrity requirement that it be genuinely immutable, enforced by permissions. Images: object storage such as S3, with only the key and metadata in the database. They are large, immutable, served directly to browsers and often through a CDN, and never queried by content. Putting the bytes in a database column inflates every backup, pollutes the buffer cache with data no query filters on, and routes every download through the application; the tradeoff is that the object store and the database can now disagree, so orphaned objects need a cleanup process. The general principle worth stating is that the access pattern - query shape, mutability, item size, read/write ratio, retention - determines the store, and the same data reshaped for a different pattern may legitimately live in two places.
follow_up_seeds: How do you keep the object store and the database from drifting apart?

text: Uploading a video triggers transcoding that takes about two minutes. Explain why this work should not happen inside the HTTP request that uploaded the file, what the API should return instead, and how the client learns that the work has finished.

expected_concepts.hint: enqueue the job, let a worker pool run it outside the request
a two-minute request ties up a connection and dies to any timeout in the path
return a job id and expose a status endpoint, or notify by webhook or push
the user gets an immediate acknowledgement and a visible progress state

common_misconceptions: proposes raising the timeouts along the path instead of decoupling the work
spawns a background thread in the web process and treats the job as safely queued
reference_answer: A two-minute request fails for structural reasons, not because it is slow. Every timeout in the path - browser, load balancer, proxy, gateway - is shorter than that, so the connection is cut and the client cannot tell whether the work succeeded. It occupies a worker or connection slot for two minutes, so a modest number of concurrent uploads exhausts the pool and takes down unrelated endpoints. A deploy or crash mid-request loses the work with no record that it was ever requested, and the client's only recovery is to retry the whole upload. It also couples two very different scaling profiles: the API is I/O-bound and the transcoder is CPU-bound, and they cannot be scaled independently while they share a process. Instead, the request should store the uploaded file, write a job record, enqueue it, and return 202 Accepted with a job id and a status URL. A separate worker pool consumes the queue. The client learns of completion by polling the status endpoint, which is simplest and adequate for a two-minute job; by a webhook if the caller is another service; or by a server-sent event or push notification for a live UI. Details worth stating: the status should distinguish queued, running, succeeded and failed, and carry the error on failure; the enqueue must be reliable, so writing the job row and enqueueing should be in one transaction or use an outbox, otherwise a crash between them loses the job silently; and a background thread in the web process is not a queue, because it dies with the process.
follow_up_seeds: What guarantees that the job is not lost between the upload and the queue?

text: A message queue guarantees at-least-once delivery, and your consumer charges a customer's card. Explain the hazard this specific combination creates, what property the consumer must therefore guarantee and how you would implement it, and the purpose of a dead-letter queue when one message keeps failing.

expected_concepts.hint: a message may be redelivered after a crash or a missed acknowledgement
processing the same message twice must have the same effect as once
a stable business key stored with a uniqueness constraint, checked in the same transaction
park a repeatedly failing message so it stops blocking or looping, and can be inspected

common_misconceptions: asks for exactly-once delivery from the broker instead of idempotent processing
deduplicates in an in-memory set, which does not survive a restart or a second consumer
reference_answer: At-least-once means the broker will redeliver whenever it cannot confirm a message was handled - the consumer crashed after charging but before acknowledging, the acknowledgement was lost, or a visibility timeout expired while the work was still running. Combined with a side effect as irreversible as a card charge, redelivery means charging the customer twice, and no amount of broker configuration removes the possibility, because the failure is in the gap between doing the work and recording that it was done. The consumer must therefore be idempotent: processing the same message twice has the same effect as processing it once. Implement it with a stable idempotency key derived from the business event rather than from the delivery - an order id, not a message id, since a retry may carry a fresh message id - stored in a table with a unique constraint, and written in the same transaction as the effect. The consumer inserts the key and does the work atomically, and a duplicate key collision means the work is already done, so acknowledge and stop. When the effect is in an external system, use that system's own idempotency key, which every payment provider offers for this exact reason. A dead-letter queue handles the other failure: a message that fails every time - malformed payload, a deleted referenced record, a bug - would otherwise be retried forever, consuming capacity and, on an ordered queue, blocking everything behind it. After a bounded number of attempts, ideally with backoff, the message is moved to the DLQ where it stops harming throughput and can be inspected, fixed and replayed. A non-empty DLQ should alert; a DLQ nobody watches is just a slower way to drop messages.

text: Service A calls service B. B slows down badly but does not return errors. Explain how a missing timeout in A turns B's slowness into A's outage, why a naive retry policy makes the situation worse rather than better, and what you would configure instead.

expected_concepts.hint: a call with no deadline holds a connection and a worker indefinitely
retries multiply load onto a dependency that is already struggling
spread retries in time and randomise them so clients do not synchronise
A's thread or connection pool exhausts, so A fails requests unrelated to B

common_misconceptions: believes retries are always safe because the request eventually succeeds
sets one global timeout without regard to the caller's own deadline
reference_answer: Without a timeout, each call to B occupies one of A's workers or connections until B eventually answers. As B slows, in-flight calls accumulate: arrival rate multiplied by response time is the concurrency required, so a tenfold slowdown needs tenfold the pool. When the pool is exhausted, A can serve nothing at all - including requests that never touch B - so B's degradation becomes A's total outage. That is a cascading failure, and the missing timeout is what propagates it. Naive retries make it worse in a specific way: retrying a slow call multiplies the load arriving at B at exactly the moment it is least able to cope, so the system applies maximum pressure to its weakest point. Worse, retries compose - three layers each retrying three times is twenty-seven calls for one request - and when many clients retry on the same schedule they synchronise into waves. What to configure: an explicit connect and read timeout on every outbound call, set from the p99 of the healthy dependency rather than from a round number; a deadline propagated from the inbound request, so a caller that has already spent its budget does not start work nobody is waiting for; a small bounded number of retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and only for idempotent operations; a retry budget capping retries as a fraction of total traffic, so retries can never dominate; a bulkhead - a separate connection pool per dependency - so B cannot consume all of A's capacity; and a circuit breaker to stop calling B when failure is the expected outcome. Failing fast is the goal: a quick error preserves capacity, whereas an unbounded wait spends it.

text: Describe what a circuit breaker does in each of its three states and what causes each transition. Then explain what your service should return to its own callers while the breaker is open, and why an error returned quickly can be better than a response that eventually succeeds.

expected_concepts.hint: closed, open and half-open, with thresholds and a probe driving the transitions
rejecting immediately preserves the caller's capacity and stops the pile-up
serve a reduced but useful response instead of an error where the feature allows
cached or default data, with the reduced confidence made explicit to the caller

common_misconceptions: describes the breaker as only two states, with no probing path back to healthy
assumes a fallback should hide the degradation from the caller entirely
reference_answer: Closed: calls pass through, and the breaker counts failures - errors and timeouts - over a rolling window. When the failure rate crosses a threshold, with a minimum request count so that two failures out of three do not trip it, it opens. Open: calls are rejected immediately without touching the dependency, which both protects the caller's resources and gives the dependency room to recover, since a struggling service that keeps receiving full traffic may never recover. After a cooldown the breaker moves to half-open. Half-open: a small number of trial calls are allowed through; if they succeed the breaker closes, and if any fails it opens again for another cooldown. Half-open is what makes recovery automatic and prevents the full load from returning in one step. While open, the right response depends on the feature. Where a degraded answer is meaningful, degrade: serve the last cached value, a default, or a partial page with the affected section absent or marked unavailable - a product page without recommendations is still a product page. Where no honest answer exists, return a clear error quickly, with a retryable status and a Retry-After if you can estimate one, so the caller can decide. The reason fast failure beats eventual success is that latency consumes resources everywhere it occurs: the caller's threads, the user's patience, the upstream's timeout budget. A request that takes thirty seconds and succeeds may have blocked capacity that would have served dozens of others, and by then the user has usually left or refreshed, which is another request. Failing fast keeps failure contained to the affected feature rather than letting it spread through the pools that everything shares - and the degradation should be visible in the response and in telemetry, not hidden, because a silently degraded system is one nobody fixes.

text: Logs, metrics and distributed traces overlap but answer different questions. For each of the three, give one question it answers well and one it answers badly, and say which you would reach for first when a single user reports that one particular request was slow.

expected_concepts.hint: events with detail, aggregates over time, and one request across services
match the signal to whether the question is about one request or about a population
metrics are cheap because they aggregate; a per-user label destroys that
a trace, found by request id, shows where the time went

common_misconceptions: adds a high-cardinality label such as user id to a metric to answer per-user questions
believes traces make logs unnecessary
reference_answer: Metrics are numeric aggregates over time. They answer 'is the error rate rising', 'what is p99 latency this week', 'are we near capacity' - and they answer badly anything about one specific request, because aggregation has discarded the individual. They are cheap precisely because of that aggregation, which is why adding a user id or a request id as a label is a mistake: cardinality explodes and the backend's cost with it. Logs are discrete events with arbitrary detail. They answer 'what exactly happened in this request', 'what was the payload that caused this exception' - and they answer badly 'what is the trend across a billion requests', since computing that from raw logs is slow and expensive. Traces follow one request across service boundaries as a tree of timed spans. They answer 'where did the time go' and 'which of the eleven services this request touched was the slow one' - and they answer badly questions about aggregate health, particularly when sampling means most requests were never traced. For one user reporting one slow request, start with the trace, provided you can find it: get a request or trace id from the report or from an access log filtered by user and time, then open that trace and read the span breakdown, which usually localises the problem in seconds. Then use logs from that trace id for the detail the spans do not carry, and metrics to decide whether this was one user's problem or the visible edge of a wider one. The practical requirement underneath all of this is correlation: a trace id propagated through every service and attached to every log line, so the three signals are three views of the same event rather than three separate systems.

text: A dashboard shows an average response time of 120 ms and the team believes the service is healthy, while support tickets say otherwise. Explain what the average is hiding, which statistic you would alert on instead, and why an alert on CPU usage would not have caught this.

expected_concepts.hint: the slowest few percent of requests are the ones users complain about
alert on p95 and p99, and watch the distribution rather than one number
alert on what users experience, not on a resource that might cause it
a long right tail barely moves the mean while affecting many real requests

common_misconceptions: believes the average is representative because most requests are fast
averages percentiles across instances or time buckets, which is not mathematically valid
reference_answer: Latency distributions have a long right tail, so the mean is dominated by the fast majority and barely moves when the tail gets much worse. If 95 percent of requests take 50 ms and 5 percent take 1.5 seconds, the average is around 120 ms and looks fine, while one request in twenty is slow enough to complain about. At scale that is an enormous number of affected requests, and it is systematically the heaviest users who hit it - the ones with the most data, the most items in a page, the most reason to matter. Alert on percentiles: p95 and p99 latency, measured per endpoint, alongside the error rate and traffic. Look at the whole distribution as a heatmap rather than a single line, because a bimodal shape - two distinct clusters - tells a different story from a uniformly shifted one, usually pointing at a cache miss path, one bad instance or one slow tenant. Two technical cautions: percentiles cannot be averaged across instances or time buckets, so they must be computed from histograms; and a p99 over all endpoints hides a single catastrophic endpoint inside a large volume of fast ones. CPU would not have caught this because it is a cause, not a symptom, and it is only one of many possible causes - the tail here is far more likely to be lock contention, an N+1 query on large accounts, garbage-collection pauses, a slow dependency or connection-pool waiting, none of which raise CPU. Alerting on causes produces both misses like this one and false alarms, since high CPU on a healthy, well-utilised service is not a problem. Alert on the symptoms users feel - latency, errors, and whether the work is getting done - and keep resource metrics for diagnosis once an alert has fired.
